paragraphs.heading: What makes an animal
paragraphs.text: Animals are many-celled, eukaryotic living things that belong to the kingdom Animalia. They eat organic material, breathe oxygen, have muscle cells and can reproduce sexually. Early in development each one grows from a hollow ball of cells called a blastula. Nearly all of them can move, and together they form a clade, meaning they all descend from one common ancestor.

paragraphs.heading: How many and how big
paragraphs.text: Scientists have described more than 1.5 million living animal species. Insects make up about 1.05 million of those, molluscs more than 85,000, and vertebrates around 65,000. One estimate puts the true number of animal species on Earth at up to 7.77 million. In size they run from 8.5 μm to 33.6 m long.

paragraphs.heading: Set apart from plants and fungi
paragraphs.text: Like plants and fungi, animals are eukaryotic, many-celled and aerobic. Unlike plants and algae, they cannot make their own food, which they have in common with fungi. They take in organic material and digest it inside the body. Animal cells sit in an extracellular matrix made of collagen and elastic glycoproteins. In plants, fungi and algae, cell walls hold cells in place instead, so they develop by steady growth.

paragraphs.heading: From egg to body plan
paragraphs.text: Animals make haploid sex cells, or gametes, through meiosis: small, mobile sperm and large, still eggs. A sperm and egg fuse into a zygote, which divides by mitosis into a blastula. In most groups the blastula then folds inward into a gastrula, which has a digestive chamber and two separate germ layers, the ectoderm outside and the endoderm inside. Usually a third layer, the mesoderm, forms between them, and these layers go on to make tissues and organs.

paragraphs.heading: Deep history
paragraphs.text: Animals first show up in the fossil record in the Ediacaran period. Most modern animal phyla appeared as sea creatures in the Cambrian explosion, which started about 539 million years ago. Researchers have identified 6,331 groups of genes shared by all living animals that may come from a single common ancestor living about 650 million years ago, in the Cryogenian period.

paragraphs.heading: Sorting the animal kingdom
paragraphs.text: The scientific study of animals is zoology, and the study of their behaviour is ethology. Aristotle split animals into those with blood and those without. In 1758 Carl Linnaeus produced the first hierarchical classification of animals, and in 1874 Ernst Haeckel separated the many-celled Metazoa from the single-celled Protozoa, which no longer count as animals. Today, methods such as molecular phylogenetics reveal how groups are related, and the kingdom is split into five major clades: Porifera, Ctenophora, Placozoa, Cnidaria and Bilateria.

paragraphs.heading: Animals and people
paragraphs.text: People rely on other animals for food such as meat, eggs and dairy, for materials such as leather, fur and wool, and as pets and working animals. Dogs were the first animal to be domesticated, and they have helped in hunting, security and war. Animals have also been part of human culture since the earliest times, from cave art and totems to myths, religion and sport.
